sections.heading: Wanting the blessings that actually last
sections.text: Lord God Almighty, I am not asking you to make me important, wealthy, or admired in this world. I am asking you to count me among the people who are truly blessed in you. Make this my steady and highest concern: to receive and treasure the gifts that come from you, that are spiritual in their nature, lasting beyond this life, and deeply satisfying when everything else proves too small.
theological_themes: Choosing spiritual and eternal blessing over earthly status, wealth, or recognition.
Seeking satisfaction in God’s lasting gifts rather than in temporary success.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes believers as already blessed in Christ with every spiritual blessing. That grounds the prayer’s desire for the kind of blessing that comes from God and lasts beyond earthly rank or possessions.
Jesus contrasts treasures stored on earth with treasures stored in heaven. This supports the prayer’s request to value eternal spiritual good above visible worldly gain.

sections.heading: Seeing myself truthfully before you
sections.text: Keep me from fooling myself about who I am. Do not let me measure my life only by what people can see. Teach me to care about my beliefs as well as my behavior, my motives as well as my actions. Search me honestly, Father, and show me what is real and what is only appearance.
theological_themes: Self-examination before God, including hidden motives and inner principles.
The need for God’s searching light because the heart can misjudge itself.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to search the heart and expose any grievous way. This directly supports the prayer’s request not to live by self-deception but to be known and corrected by God.
God tells Samuel that he looks at the heart, not merely outward appearance. The prayer follows that same concern by asking to be judged not only by visible conduct but also by inward motives.

sections.heading: Not confusing emotion with renewal
sections.text: Help me not to mistake strong feelings, religious excitement, or passing impulses for the real work of your Holy Spirit. Do not let me judge my faith by occasional moments of intensity. Let the truth of my life be seen in the steady direction of my heart, in the fruit your Spirit grows over time, and in the habits that increasingly line up with you.
theological_themes: Distinguishing temporary religious emotion from genuine spiritual renewal.
The Holy Spirit’s renewing work is shown in enduring fruit and a changed disposition.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the fruit of the Spirit as the evidence of life by the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s concern that true religion is not measured by impulses but by the Spirit’s ongoing work in character.
Jesus teaches that a tree is known by its fruit. The passage helps frame the prayer’s desire to assess spiritual reality by the settled pattern and fruit of life, not by isolated impressions.

sections.heading: Living in a way that fits the gospel
sections.text: Make my heart right with you, and make my daily life worthy of the good news I claim to believe. Keep my eyes on the better country you have promised. Teach me to admit, without resentment, that I am a stranger and traveler here. This world is not my final home, so help me hold it with open hands and walk toward you with hope.
theological_themes: Integrity between the heart and outward life.
Living as a pilgrim whose final home is with God.
A gospel-shaped life that reflects heavenly citizenship.

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges believers to live in a manner worthy of the gospel. That supports the prayer’s request for a life that matches the gospel rather than merely professing it.

Hebrews describes believers who confessed they were strangers and exiles on the earth while seeking a better, heavenly country. This directly illuminates the prayer’s pilgrim language and eternal focus.

sections.heading: Needing your help for the journey
sections.text: Give me the direction, protection, strength, and comfort I need for the road from here to my final home. Keep my mind anchored in you when I am tired, confused, or afraid. Hold me steady when circumstances shift and when I cannot see what you are doing.
theological_themes: Dependence on God’s guidance and keeping care through life’s journey.
Peace and stability that come from a mind fixed on God.

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah connects steadfast peace with a mind stayed on God and trust in him. This closely supports the prayer’s request for inward steadiness amid uncertainty.
The psalm speaks of the Lord keeping his people in their going out and coming in. It fits the prayer’s appeal for divine protection and support along the whole journey.

sections.heading: Depending on the Spirit of Jesus in everything
sections.text: Give me a generous supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Make me ready for whatever obedience today requires. Teach me to love you in every mercy you give, to submit to you in every trial you allow, to trust you when I have to walk in the dark, and to find my peace in you through all the changes of life.
theological_themes: Dependence on the Spirit of Christ for obedience, endurance, and peace.
Receiving mercies with love, trials with surrender, darkness with trust, and change with stability in God.

scripture_references.connection: Paul speaks of help coming through prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ as he faces uncertain circumstances. This grounds the prayer’s request for the Spirit’s provision for duty, trial, and endurance.

Paul learns that Christ’s grace is sufficient and that weakness becomes a place where Christ’s power rests on him. This supports the prayer’s desire to submit in trials and rely on God’s strength rather than visible ease.

sections.heading: Asking you to strengthen my weak faith
sections.text: Lord, I do believe. Help me where my faith is mixed with fear, hesitation, and uncertainty. Strengthen my trust in you, not because I am steady in myself, but because you are faithful and patient with weak people like me.
theological_themes: Honest faith that brings its weakness to God.
God’s patience and help for believers who struggle with unbelief.

scripture_references.connection: The father in the Gospel asks Jesus to help his unbelief while still coming to him in faith. This directly supports the prayer’s final confession of real but needy faith.
Jesus tells Peter that he has prayed for his faith not to fail, even before Peter’s collapse. This shows Christ’s mercy toward weak believers and supports asking God to sustain faith under pressure.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original contrasts genuine spiritual renewal with the excitement of the passions. I preserved that distinction without implying that emotions are bad in themselves; the issue is mistaking temporary intensity for the Holy Spirit’s lasting work.

The language of being a stranger and pilgrim can be misunderstood as contempt for created life or earthly responsibilities. I rendered it as holding the world with open hands and looking toward the promised final home, while still living faithfully now.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “constant and prevailing disposition” as the settled direction, fruit, and habits of a person’s life rather than moment-by-moment emotional consistency.
I rendered “another and better world” as the believer’s final home and better country, drawing on Hebrews 11, rather than making the prayer mainly about escaping present life.
I kept “supply of the Spirit of Jesus” close to Philippians 1:19 and expressed it as dependence on the Spirit for obedience, endurance, trust, and peace.
